check.why: The War on Poverty was part of the Great Society's aim to reduce poverty.

check.q: Who does Medicare help?
check.why: Medicare pays for health care for people 65 and older.

check.q: How did the Immigration Act of 1965 change the country?
choices: It ended old quotas, so more immigrants came from Asia and Latin America
It required immigrants to join the army
check.why: The law ended quotas favoring northern and western Europe, making America more diverse.

lessons.title: Black Power and a Nation in Pain
lessons.mainIdea: Some Black leaders called for Black Power and self-defense, cities erupted in unrest, and King was assassinated in 1968.
reading: Not every Black leader agreed with nonviolence. *Malcolm X*, a minister in the Nation of Islam, spoke about Black pride and the right to defend oneself. He criticized the goal of integration at first. After a trip to Mecca in 1964, he began to speak of cooperation among people of all races. He was assassinated in New York in February 1965.

By 1966, some young activists, like Stokely Carmichael of SNCC, called for *Black Power*. It meant Black communities controlling their own schools, businesses and politics, and taking pride in Black culture and history. In Oakland, California, the Black Panther Party formed. It carried guns to watch the police and also ran free breakfast programs for children.

The movement moved north, too. In 1966, King lived for a time in an apartment on Chicago's West Side and led marches for fair housing. White crowds threw rocks at the marchers. Summer after summer, frustration over poverty, police treatment and discrimination exploded into *riots* in cities like Los Angeles, Newark and Detroit.

A commission appointed by President Johnson studied the riots. Its 1968 report said the main cause was racism and unequal conditions in cities. That April, King was assassinated in Memphis. A week later, Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, banning discrimination in buying and renting homes.

words.d: a Black leader who spoke about Black pride and self-defense and was killed in 1965
a movement for Black communities to control their own institutions and take pride in their culture
violent, disorderly outbreaks by crowds, often with property destroyed

look.title: A Warning From a Commission
look.text: Our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal.
look.cite: Report of the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders (the Kerner Commission), 1968
look.prompt: This report came from a government commission, not from protesters. Why might that make its warning more powerful?

check.q: What did “Black Power” mean to many of its supporters?
choices: Black communities controlling their own institutions and taking pride in their culture
check.why: Black Power stressed self-reliance, community control and pride in Black culture.

check.q: What did King do in Chicago in 1966?
choices: He led the Montgomery Bus Boycott
He lived on the West Side and led marches for fair housing
He gave the “I Have a Dream” speech
check.why: King moved into a West Side apartment and marched for open housing in Chicago.

check.q: What did the Kerner Commission say was the main cause of the riots?
choices: Racism and unequal conditions in cities
check.why: The 1968 report blamed racism and unequal conditions for the unrest.

lessons.title: Farmworkers and Latino Rights
lessons.mainIdea: César Chávez, Dolores Huerta and Filipino American workers led farmworkers in a nonviolent struggle for fair pay and better conditions.
reading: Farmworkers picked much of America's food, but they were among the lowest-paid workers in the country. Many were Mexican American or Filipino American. They worked long days in the hot sun, often without clean water, bathrooms or protection from pesticides. They moved from farm to farm and had little power.

*César Chávez* had worked in the fields since he was a boy. In 1962, he and *Dolores Huerta* started a union for farmworkers. In 1965, Filipino American grape pickers led by Larry Itliong went on strike in Delano, California. Chávez and Huerta's union joined them. Together they became the United Farm Workers.

Like King, Chávez believed in nonviolence. The strikers marched and asked Americans to stop buying grapes. Millions joined the *boycott*. Chávez also went on long fasts, refusing food for weeks, to draw attention to the cause. In 1970, many grape growers finally signed contracts giving workers better pay and conditions. Huerta's rallying cry, “Sí, se puede,” means “Yes, it can be done.”

Other Latino Americans also pushed for change. In 1968, thousands of Mexican American students in Los Angeles walked out of their high schools to demand better schools and classes that taught their history. In Chicago, young Puerto Ricans in a group called the Young Lords organized to fight for better housing and services in their neighborhoods.

words.d: a leader who organized farmworkers into a union and used nonviolent protest
a co-founder of the farmworkers' union and a lifelong organizer
refusing to buy something as a protest
a group of workers who join together to bargain for better pay and conditions

look.title: Grapes at the Grocery Store
look.text: It is 1968. Your family is shopping in Chicago. A young woman outside the store hands out flyers. She asks shoppers not to buy California grapes until the workers who pick them get fair pay and safe conditions. The workers are two thousand miles away, but your choice at the store is part of their strike.

lessons.title: Equal Rights for Women
lessons.mainIdea: The women's movement challenged unfair treatment at work and in school and won new laws such as Title IX.
reading: In the 1950s and early 1960s, many women were expected to stay home as wives and mothers. Women who worked often earned much less than men for the same job. Many colleges, medical schools and law schools accepted few women. Newspapers listed jobs under “Help Wanted—Male” and “Help Wanted—Female.”

In 1963, Betty Friedan wrote a book called *The Feminine Mystique*. It described women who felt unhappy and unfulfilled with lives limited to the home. The book sold millions of copies. The same year, Congress passed the Equal Pay Act, which required equal pay for men and women doing the same work. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 also banned job discrimination based on sex.

In 1966, Friedan and others formed the National Organization for Women, or NOW, to push for *equal rights*. In 1968, Shirley Chisholm of New York became the first Black woman elected to Congress. In 1972, Congress passed *Title IX*, which banned sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money. Girls' sports teams grew quickly as a result.

Congress also passed the Equal Rights Amendment in 1972 and sent it to the states. Supporters said it would guarantee equality for women in the Constitution. Opponents, including many women, argued it could take away protections women already had. Not enough states ratified it by the deadline, so it did not become part of the Constitution.

the same rights and chances for everyone under the law

lessons.title: Native Nations and Disability Rights
lessons.mainIdea: Native Americans demanded respect for their treaties and self-rule, and people with disabilities began a movement for equal access.
reading: Native Americans had faced termination and relocation in the 1950s. In the 1960s, many young Native people pushed back. In 1968, activists in Minneapolis formed the *American Indian Movement*, or AIM. They fought police mistreatment and demanded that the U.S. honor its treaties.

In 1969, a group called Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay for more than a year and a half. They said it should become a Native cultural center. In 1973, AIM members occupied Wounded Knee, South Dakota, the site of the 1890 massacre, for 71 days. In 1970, President Nixon ended termination and supported *self-determination*, the right of tribes to govern themselves.

People with disabilities also began to organize. Many were shut out of schools, jobs and buildings with stairs and no ramps. Starting in the late 1940s, the University of Illinois became a leader in opening college to students who used wheelchairs. It added ramps and accessible buses, and it started wheelchair sports teams.

In the 1960s, Ed Roberts, who used a wheelchair and a breathing machine, fought to attend the University of California, Berkeley. He helped start the *independent living* movement. In 1973, Congress passed a law banning discrimination against people with disabilities in programs that receive federal money. In 1975, another law promised children with disabilities a free public education. That law is the root of today's IEPs.

words.d: a Native American rights group founded in 1968
the right of a people, such as a Native nation, to govern themselves
the idea that people with disabilities should make their own choices and live in their communities

lessons.title: Why America Went to Vietnam
lessons.mainIdea: The U.S. became involved in Vietnam to stop communism from spreading in Southeast Asia, based on the domino theory.
reading: Vietnam, in Southeast Asia, was a French colony for many years. After World War II, a communist leader named *Ho Chi Minh* led a war for independence against France. In 1954, the Vietnamese defeated the French at a battle called Dien Bien Phu. A peace agreement split Vietnam in two, with a communist North and a non-communist South.

The agreement called for an election in 1956 to reunite the country. The South's leader, Ngo Dinh Diem, refused to hold it, fearing Ho Chi Minh would win. The United States backed Diem. Communist fighters in the South, called the *Viet Cong*, began a war against his government with help from the North.

American leaders believed in the *domino theory*. They feared that if Vietnam fell to communism, nearby countries would fall one after another, like a row of dominoes. Presidents Eisenhower and Kennedy sent money, weapons and military advisers to South Vietnam. By 1963, about 16,000 American advisers were there.

Many Vietnamese saw the war differently. To them, it was a long fight for independence from foreign control, first from France and then from the United States. This difference in how each side saw the war helps explain why it was so hard for the U.S. to win.

words.d: the communist leader of North Vietnam who fought for Vietnam's independence
communist fighters in South Vietnam who fought against the South's government and the U.S.
the idea that if one country fell to communism, its neighbors would fall too

lessons.title: Escalation and the Tet Offensive
lessons.mainIdea: After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, the U.S. sent hundreds of thousands of troops, but the 1968 Tet Offensive made many Americans doubt the war could be won.
reading: In August 1964, the U.S. said North Vietnamese boats had attacked American Navy ships in the Gulf of Tonkin. Congress quickly passed the *Gulf of Tonkin Resolution*. It allowed the president to take all necessary steps to defend U.S. forces. Johnson used it to widen the war without a formal declaration of war.

In 1965, the U.S. began heavy bombing of North Vietnam and sent combat troops to South Vietnam. This growth of the war is called *escalation*. The number of American troops rose year after year. Many were drafted, and young men from poor and working-class families served in large numbers.

The fighting was hard. The Viet Cong used *guerrilla warfare*: small groups who attacked by surprise and then disappeared into jungles, villages and tunnels. It was hard for American soldiers to tell friend from enemy. Bombing and chemicals like Agent Orange harmed the land and many civilians.

Night after night, TV news showed the war. In January 1968, the Tet Offensive struck cities across South Vietnam. U.S. forces pushed the attackers back, but Americans were shocked. Leaders had said the war was nearly won. Many people began to believe the government had not told the truth. This lack of trust was called a *credibility gap*.

fighting by small groups using surprise attacks, then hiding

lessons.title: Protest and the War's End
lessons.mainIdea: A growing antiwar movement divided the nation, and President Nixon slowly withdrew U.S. troops, ending American fighting in 1973.
reading: As the war grew, so did protest. College students held teach-ins and marches. Some young men burned their draft cards. Boxer Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted and lost his title for years. Other Americans supported the war and saw protesters as disloyal. People who backed the war were called *hawks*, and those who opposed it were called *doves*.

Even students in junior high took a stand. In 1965, Mary Beth Tinker, age 13, and other students in Des Moines, Iowa, wore black armbands to school to mourn the war's dead. They were suspended. In *Tinker v. Des Moines* in 1969, the Supreme Court ruled that students have the right to peaceful free speech at school.

President Nixon promised to end the war. His plan, called *Vietnamization*, was to train South Vietnam's army to take over the fighting while American troops came home. But in 1970 he also sent troops into neighboring Cambodia. Protests erupted. At Kent State University in Ohio, National Guard soldiers fired on students, killing four. Days later, police killed two students at Jackson State College in Mississippi.

Many said that if 18-year-olds could be drafted, they should be able to vote. In 1971, the 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18. In January 1973, a peace agreement was signed, and the last U.S. combat troops left that spring. In 1975, North Vietnam conquered the South. More than 58,000 Americans and well over a million Vietnamese died in the war.
